introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
> "A monopoly in the strictest sense, occurs when a single firm or small group of firms who coordinate their activities, control the entire market supply of a good or service. **Sometimes, a monopoly will be able to supply the same good in different markets at different prices for reasons not related to costs or quality differences.** In the U. K for example, a firm is regarded as a monopoly if it controls 25percent of the total market supply of a particular good or service. An important feature of monopoly is its ability to make decisions about price. Economists are interested in monopoly primarily because of its effects on the allocation of resources".

*Source: Adapted from Introductory Economics by Barry Harrison, Charles Smith and Brinley Davies, page 94.*
incertitudes: La phrase soulignée dans le sujet imprimé (« Sometimes, a monopoly will be able to supply the same good in different markets at different prices... ») est transcrite en gras, le souligné n'existant pas en Markdown ; la coquille imprimée « 25percent » est conservée telle quelle.

Question 3(c)(i) : « economically efficient » n'est pas défini dans le sujet ; le corrigé l'entend comme efficacité productive (coûts moyens bas grâce aux économies d'échelle) et dynamique (innovation), seul sens dans lequel un monopole peut être jugé efficace.

Question 3(d) : « operates in public interest » est lu comme « les raisons pour lesquelles un monopole peut servir l'intérêt général » ; les raisons données sont indicatives (barème 1 point par raison, quatre exigées).

Aucun total n'est imprimé par question (« All questions carry equal marks ») : `points` de l'exercice est laissé vide ; les points de chaque sous-question (a), (b)... sont la somme des points imprimés de ses parties ; la somme des points imprimés de chaque question vaut 20.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Which economic term best describes the underlined sentence in the passage? (2 marks)

(ii) List 2 necessary conditions for a monopoly to operate successfully as explained in the underlined sentence in the passage. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The underlined sentence describes **price discrimination**: selling the same good (or service) to different buyers or in different markets at different prices, for reasons not related to differences in cost.

**(ii)** Two necessary conditions (any two, 2 marks each, with explanation):

1. **The firm must have monopoly power (be a price-maker).** It must control the supply, so that it can set the price instead of accepting the market price. Under perfect competition a firm cannot charge two different prices.
2. **The markets must be kept separate (no resale).** Buyers in the cheap market must not be able to resell to buyers in the dear market, otherwise the difference in price disappears. Separation may be by geography, time (peak and off-peak), age or use, or because the good is a personal service.
3. **The elasticity of demand must differ between the markets.** The monopolist charges the higher price where demand is inelastic and the lower price where demand is elastic; this raises total revenue and profit.

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify 4 sources of monopoly power. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Monopoly power comes from **barriers to the entry of other firms** into the market. Four sources (1 mark each, any four):

1. **Control of essential raw materials or resources** (e.g. a firm that owns all the known deposits of a mineral).
2. **Patents, copyrights and licences**: the law gives the inventor or licence-holder the sole right to produce.
3. **Government action (legal monopoly)**: the state grants the sole right to supply a service or creates a state-owned monopoly, as with electricity, water or posts.
4. **Economies of scale (natural monopoly)**: large firms have much lower unit costs, so a new small firm cannot compete; one large firm can serve the whole market most cheaply.
5. **Mergers, takeovers and collusion** that remove rivals and bring a large share of the market under one control.
6. **Strong brand loyalty, heavy advertising or high start-up costs** that discourage new entrants.

questions.enonce_markdown:
When is a monopoly described to be:

(i) economically efficient? (2 marks)

(ii) allocatively inefficient? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A monopoly is economically efficient** when it uses the **large scale of production to produce at a lower average cost** than many small firms could. This is the case of a **natural monopoly** (electricity or water supply, railways), where **economies of scale** are so great that one firm can supply the whole market at the lowest cost. It is also efficient when it passes lower costs to consumers as lower prices (or is regulated to do so), and when its supernormal profits are used to finance research and development and new products (**dynamic efficiency**).

**(ii) A monopoly is allocatively inefficient** when it **sets a price above marginal cost ($P > MC$) and restricts output** below the level that perfect competition would produce. Allocative efficiency requires $P = MC$, i.e. that the price consumers pay equals the cost to society of the last unit produced. Because the monopolist maximises profit where $MR = MC$ and then charges the higher price shown by the demand curve, consumers value the last unit more than it costs to produce, so **too few resources are allocated to the product**. The result is a **loss of consumer surplus (deadweight loss)** and higher prices.

questions.enonce_markdown: List four reasons to justify that a monopolist operates in public interest. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Four reasons (1 mark each; any four of the following):

1. **Economies of scale**: a large monopolist produces at low unit cost, which can mean lower prices to consumers.
2. **Natural monopoly**: for public utilities (water, electricity, railways) one supplier avoids the wasteful duplication of networks.
3. **Research and development**: supernormal profits finance research and innovation, giving new and better products and techniques.
4. **Cross-subsidisation of services**: profits from some activities can keep going services that would otherwise be unprofitable, such as postal or transport services to remote rural areas.
5. **Stability of supply and prices**: a single supplier can plan output and smooth fluctuations in prices and supply.
6. **Strength against foreign competitors**: a large national firm can compete on world markets and earn foreign exchange.

questions.enonce_markdown: State two ways by which the government can control monopoly. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two ways (1 mark each):

1. **Anti-monopoly (competition) legislation and regulatory bodies**: laws that forbid abuse of market power and restrict mergers and takeovers that would create a monopoly, enforced by a competition commission.
2. **Price control (price cap)**: the government fixes a maximum price a monopolist may charge, ideally close to marginal cost.
3. **Taxation of monopoly profits**: a lump-sum or profit tax reduces supernormal profits.
4. **Nationalisation (public ownership)** of the monopoly so that it is run in the public interest.
5. **Encouraging competition**: removing barriers to entry (deregulation, ending exclusive licences) or breaking the monopoly into smaller firms.
